questions.stem: What does a polynomial-time reduction from problem A to problem B imply?

options.text: Problem B can be solved in polynomial time if A can be.
Problem A is easier than problem B.
Problem A is NP-complete.
Problem B is NP-complete.

questions.explanation: A polynomial-time reduction implies that if we have an efficient solution for problem B, we can use it to solve problem A efficiently. It does not imply anything about the complexity of A or B individually.

questions.stem: Consider a 3-SAT instance with 4 clauses and 6 variables. If reduced to a CLIQUE problem, what is the size of the clique needed to satisfy the instance? Provide your answer as an integer.
questions.explanation: In the reduction from 3-SAT to CLIQUE, each clause corresponds to a vertex in the graph. A satisfying assignment corresponds to a clique of size equal to the number of clauses, which is 4 in this case.

questions.stem: Explain why showing a polynomial-time reduction from a known NP-complete problem to another problem is sufficient to prove the latter is NP-complete.
markingGuide: State that the problem must also be in NP.
Explain that solving the new problem efficiently implies solving the NP-complete problem efficiently.
Mention that this establishes the new problem as being at least as hard as the NP-complete problem.
questions.explanation: To prove a problem is NP-complete, it must be in NP and be at least as hard as any NP problem. By reducing a known NP-complete problem to it, we show that solving the new problem efficiently would solve the NP-complete problem efficiently, thus proving its NP-completeness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a key characteristic of NP-complete problems?

options.text: They can be solved in polynomial time.
They are the hardest problems in NP.
They have no known solutions.
They are easier than NP-hard problems.

questions.explanation: NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP, meaning that if any NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, all problems in NP can be solved in polynomial time.

questions.stem: Describe the steps involved in reducing the Hamiltonian Cycle problem to the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) to show that TSP is NP-complete.
markingGuide: Define the Hamiltonian Cycle problem and its goal.
Explain how to construct a TSP instance from a Hamiltonian Cycle instance.
Discuss how a solution to the TSP instance implies a solution to the Hamiltonian Cycle instance.
questions.explanation: The Hamiltonian Cycle problem involves finding a cycle that visits each vertex exactly once. To reduce it to TSP, we construct a TSP instance where cities correspond to vertices and distances are 1 for edges in the graph and 2 otherwise. A TSP tour of length equal to the number of vertices implies a Hamiltonian cycle.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between NP-hard and NP-complete problems?

options.text: All NP-complete problems are NP-hard.
All NP-hard problems are NP-complete.
NP-complete problems are easier than NP-hard problems.
NP-hard problems can be solved in polynomial time.

questions.explanation: NP-complete problems are a subset of NP-hard problems. They are both in NP and as hard as the hardest problems in NP, making them NP-hard by definition.
